impactors.name: Theia (Moon-forming impactor)
impactors.blurb: A Mars-sized world, Theia, grew in the inner Solar System as Earth's neighbour, perhaps closer to the Sun. About 4.5 billion years ago it struck the young Earth; the debris became the Moon.

path.note: Theia accretes in the inner Solar System near Earth's orbit (iron isotopes: all of Theia is inner-Solar-System material, possibly from closer to the Sun than Earth). Formation time is not measured; assumed within a few Myr of CAIs (4567.3 Ma), unsourced. ~1 AU from proto-Earth.

Neighbouring orbit. If co-orbital at L4/L5 (Belbruno & Gott hypothesis) the distance is exactly 1 AU; on a neighbouring orbit at ~0.7-0.9 AU it swings between ~0.1 and ~1.9 AU. Drawn as the orbit-averaged ~1 AU.

Orbit destabilised; approaches on a slow, near-zero-energy (near-parabolic) path. The timing of the final approach is not known; drawn ~0.5 Myr before impact at ~0.07 AU (1e10 m) only so the line visibly turns in.

Collision: the path joins the inner track (Earth). The inner track is human scale by convention (MatterScale.InnerMetres = 1 m, log10 = 0); physical contact happens at a centre separation of R_Earth + R_Theia ~ 6.4e6 + 3.4e6 m ~ 9.8e6 m (log10 6.99). Date: 4.51 Ga (Apollo zircons; matches matter.json). Published range 4.51-4.35 Ga; Hf-W gives ~50 Myr after CAIs (~4.52 Ga); magma-ocean model 4.425 +/- 0.025 Ga; a 2024 study reads the 4.35 Ga ages as remelting, favouring an old Moon.

impactors.name: Late Heavy Bombardment: asteroid shaken loose by the giant planets
impactors.blurb: In the classic picture, a shift of the giant planets about 4 billion years ago scattered asteroids and outer bodies inward, cratering the Moon and Earth. Whether this was a spike or the tail of a long decline is debated.

path.note: Forms in the asteroid belt (~2.2-3.3 AU), 2-3 Myr after CAIs; orbit-averaged distance from Earth ~2 AU.
Stable in the belt for ~600 Myr.

Giant-planet migration/instability (Nice model) strongly perturbs the belt. 'The cataclysm should have started ~3.95Gy ago' (Morbidelli et al. 2018, under one assumption); the instability's date is itself debated.

Collision: the path joins the inner track (Earth). The inner track is human scale by convention (MatterScale.InnerMetres = 1 m, log10 = 0); physical contact happens at a centre separation of R_Earth + r ~ 6.4e6 m (log10 6.80). Date: Imbrium basin ~3.9 Ga (Apollo samples). The epoch marker sits at 4.1 Ga; proposed span 4.1-3.8 Ga (spike) or ~4.2-3.4 Ga (prolonged).

impactors.name: Late Heavy Bombardment: leftover planetesimal (accretion tail)
impactors.blurb: The newer view: no spike, just the long tail of planet building. Rocky leftovers near Earth's own orbit kept hitting the Moon and Earth, the last big basins forming about 3.9 billion years ago.

path.note: A rocky planetesimal left over at ~0.5-1.5 AU after terrestrial planet accretion (Nesvorny et al. 2023); typical distance from Earth ~0.5 AU.
Survives on a planet-crossing orbit while the population declines; distance swings widely, drawn as ~0.5 AU.

Collision: the path joins the inner track (Earth). The inner track is human scale by convention (MatterScale.InnerMetres = 1 m, log10 = 0); physical contact happens at a centre separation of R_Earth + r ~ 6.4e6 m (log10 6.80). Date: Imbrium ~3.9 Ga; in this model a late Imbrium has a ~15-35% probability. Comets contribute insignificantly.

impactors.name: Chicxulub impactor
impactors.blurb: A carbonaceous asteroid 10-14 km wide, born beyond Jupiter in the Solar System's first few million years, parked in the asteroid belt for 4.5 billion years, then struck Mexico 66 million years ago. The dark, cold years that followed ended the non-avian dinosaurs.

path.note: Forms beyond Jupiter (ruthenium isotopes: carbonaceous-type), as chondrite parent bodies did 2-3 Myr after CAIs (4567.3 Ma). C-type bodies came from a broad 5-20 AU region; drawn at ~8 AU from the 1 AU region where Earth would form (Earth itself did not exist yet).

Scattered inward during Jupiter and Saturn's gas accretion and captured in the outer main belt while the gas disk was present (first few Myr). Implantation is a model (Raymond & Izidoro 2017), not measured for this body.

Resides in the main belt for ~4.5 Gyr, quite likely (~60%) beyond 2.5 AU. The real distance from Earth swings between ~1.5 and ~4.3 AU every ~1.3-1.5 years (log10 11.35-11.81); drawn as the ~3 AU average.

Leaves the belt, presumably by Yarkovsky drift into a resonance. When is unknown: the Baptistina breakup (proposed 160 Ma) is ruled out by composition (LL, not carbonaceous) and age. Mean near-Earth lifetime of >5 km bodies is ~1.2 Myr (range 0.1-100 Myr), so ~1 Myr before impact is typical, not known.
Near-Earth orbit; typical distance ~1 AU, swinging widely.

Collision: the path joins the inner track (Earth). The inner track is human scale by convention (MatterScale.InnerMetres = 1 m, log10 = 0); physical contact happens at a centre separation of R_Earth + r ~ 6.38e6 m (log10 6.80). Date 66.038 Ma (40Ar/39Ar; matter.json rounds to 66.0 Ma). Struck at ~20 km/s (the average asteroid encounter speed; 18 km/s in crater models), steeply (45-60 deg) from the northeast, at the Yucatan, making a ~180-200 km crater.
